questions.q: Why is a blue-green rollback as fast as the original cutover, per this lesson?
options: Because the old (blue) environment never stopped running, so flipping routing back is just a routing change
Because blue-green deployments don't require a load balancer
Because the new version is automatically deleted after deployment
Because blue-green rollbacks skip the registry entirely
questions.explain: Blue never stopped running during the cutover, so rolling back is the same kind of instant routing switch as the original cutover.

questions.q: Why is a rolling-update rollback typically gradual rather than instant?
options: Because rolling updates don't support rollback at all
Because it has to wait for a second full environment to be built first
Because it runs the same instance-by-instance process in reverse, taking roughly as long as the forward rollout did
Because the load balancer must be manually reconfigured for each instance
questions.explain: A rolling-update rollback swaps instances back one at a time, the same way the rollout went forward -- so it takes similar time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what can make a rollback actually break data instead of fixing a bad release?
options: Rolling back during business hours instead of overnight
Using blue-green instead of a rolling update
Having too many container instances running
A schema change in the new release that the old code isn't backward-compatible with
questions.explain: If the new version changed the database schema and the old code can't handle that schema, rolling the app back without also reversing the schema change can break things further.

questions.q: What AI-specific rollback case does this lesson describe that a plain web app doesn't have?
options: AI apps can never be rolled back once deployed
Rolling back the model/weights independently of the application code, since either one can be the actual problem
AI apps only support rollback through blue-green, never rolling updates
AI apps require a manual database migration on every rollback
questions.explain: A bad release can be bad code with a fine model, a fine code with a bad model, or both -- and the lesson's point is these are tracked and rolled back independently.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does detection matter more than the rollback mechanism itself?
options: Because a fast rollback mechanism is worthless if the problem takes an hour to even notice
Because detection replaces the need for any rollback mechanism at all
Because rollback mechanisms are identical regardless of detection speed
Because only blue-green deployments require detection, not rolling updates
questions.explain: A thirty-second rollback mechanism doesn't help if nothing triggers it for an hour -- automated detection has to come first.
